newsitem.title: USA: Ex-Texaco official charged with obstructing justice. [CORRECTED 00:45 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Ex-Texaco official charged with obstructing justice. [CORRECTED 00:45 GMT]

text.p: Former Texaco Inc. executive Richard Lundwall was charged by federal authorities on Tuesday with destroying crucial evidence in connection with a racial discrimination lawsuit against the oil company.

The criminal charge was the latest blow against the United States' third-largest oil company, which faces a nationwide boycott due to allegations it discriminated against black and other minority employees.
The charge of obstructing justice arose from a lawsuit against Texaco by a group of black employees accusing the company of systematically discriminating against blacks and denying them promotions.

Texaco on Friday reached a $176 million settlement of the 1994 lawsuit -- the biggest settlement of a discrimination case in the United States. The lawsuit originally sought payments totalling $71 million.

Lundwall, 55, the former senior coordinator of personnel services in Texaco's finance department, shredded or purged documents critical to the lawsuit, court papers released Tuesday alleged. Texaco settled the lawsuit shortly after transcripts were
made public of conversations recorded during a 1994 meeting at which Texaco executives allegedly discussed destroying evidence and also used expletives and apparent racist terms.

Lundwall, who secretly recorded conversations during the meeting and later turned over tapes to plaintiffs in the discrimination lawsuit, was released on his own recognisance (corrects terms of release from "was released on a $50,000 bond").
He did not enter a plea during the brief hearing before U.S. Magistrate Lisa Margaret Smith. If convicted, he faces up to 10 years in prison and a $250,000 fine.
A hearing was set for Dec. 18 in federal court in White Plains, N.Y., the New York City suburb where Texaco is headquartered.
Lundwall, who lost his job in August in a restructuring at Texaco, was one of four former or current executives disciplined by Texaco in connection with the 1994 meeting.

Lundwall spoke little during Tuesday's hearing, except to acknowledge that he understood the magistrate's instructions and to say he had taken medication the night before to help him sleep. He lives in Danbury, Conn.
As he left the courthouse, he told reporters, "I'd love to share information with all of you, but at this point I can't."

Lundwall's attorney, Christopher Riley, said he found it "ironic" that Lundwall was the first Texaco executive charged in the case even though his client had been cooperating and had turned over the tapes to plaintiffs in the lawsuit.
Texaco said that if he destroyed documents, Lundwall had violated company policy.

"If Mr. Lundwall did what he was charged with, he was acting in direct violation of expressed company policy as well as written instructions from the company's general consul to preserve all documents relating to the discrimination lawsuit," Texaco spokesman James Swords said.
Swords said Texaco was cooperating with the U.S. attorney in the investigation but declined to elaborate.
The company suspended two current employees with pay and suspended the benefits of Lundwall and another retired executive allegedly involved in the 1994 meeting.

Despite settlement of the discrimination lawsuit, several civil rights leaders, including the Rev. Jesse Jackson, called for a Texaco boycott. They also called for Texaco stockholders to sell their stock in the company.
Texaco shares rose $1.625 to $100 Tuesday on the New York Stock Exchange.
